Architecture and number of parameters - Yes
Interaction with hardware or software - Yes
License - Yes
Samples of outlier training data - No

The answer confirms disclosure of number of parameters under Annex XII, point 1, which requires model architecture and parameter count.
The answer affirms disclosure of interaction with hardware, citing Annex XII, point 1, which requires description of such interaction.
The answer confirms license disclosure as part of the general description in Annex XII, point 1.

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: No, "healthcare decision making" is not one of the high-risk areas; Annex III contains no healthcare area as such, although several individual healthcare-related use-cases fall inside other Annex III areas and clinical AI can be high-risk by the separate Annex I product route. Under Article 6(2) an AI system is high-risk where it falls within a use-case listed under one of the eight areas of Annex III: biometrics (Annex III.1); critical infrastructure (Annex III.2); education and vocational training (Annex III.3); employment, workers' management and access to self-employment (Annex III.4); access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits (Annex III.5); law enforcement (Annex III.6); migration, asylum and border control management (Annex III.7); and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III.8). An area is only the numbered heading, high-risk status attaches to the lettered use-cases beneath it, not to the sector at large. Healthcare appears inside Annex III.5 through three specific use-cases: systems used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them (Annex III.5(a)); systems for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in life and health insurance (Annex III.5(c)); and systems to evaluate and classify emergency calls or to dispatch or prioritise emergency first response services, including emergency healthcare patient triage systems (Annex III.5(d)). Clinical or diagnostic decision-support outside those entries is not high-risk via Annex III; it is caught, if at all, by the Annex I product route under Article 6(1), where the AI system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation, including Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices (Annex I.11) and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices (Annex I.12), and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Two qualifications complete the picture. A system that does fall within an Annex III use-case escapes high-risk classification under the Article 6(3) derogation where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and it performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without being meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review, or performs a preparatory task, but it is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons. Second, the absence of a healthcare area is not permanent: under Article 7(1) the Commission may by delegated act adopted in accordance with Article 97 add or modify use-cases where cumulatively the systems are intended to be used in an area already listed in Annex III and pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, equivalent to or greater than that of the systems already listed; that power cannot create a new area.

No

The answer explicitly states 'No' and explains that healthcare decision making is not a standalone high-risk area in Annex III, which aligns with the correct interpretation of the regulation.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Introducing guardrails cannot move an AI system out of the high-risk class; changing its capabilities and intended use can, but only where the change takes the system genuinely outside the classification rules in Article 6, not merely reduces its residual risk. The Regulation contains no "moderate risk" tier that mitigation earns a system. Classification is binary and purpose-driven: a system is high-risk either on the Annex I product-safety route or because its intended purpose falls within one of the lettered use-cases under Annex III's eight areas (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes). Guardrails are a consequence of that classification, not an exit from it. Article 8(1) makes this explicit: high-risk systems must comply with the Section 2 requirements taking into account their intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art, and the Article 9 risk-management system is to be taken into account when ensuring compliance with those requirements, mitigation operates inside the regime. The same is true of the Article 9 duties to identify foreseeable risks, estimate risks emerging under misuse, evaluate post-market data and adopt targeted risk-control measures, and of the instructions-for-use duties in Article 13(3)(b)(ii), (iii) to disclose the tested level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and the circumstances, in intended use or under reasonably foreseeable misuse, that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights. Guardrails discharge these obligations; they presuppose them. That mitigation measures can bear on risk classification at all is confined to the Commission. Article 7(2)(k) directs the Commission, when assessing the Article 7(1)(b) condition, to weigh the extent to which existing Union law provides effective measures of redress (excluding damages claims) and effective measures to prevent or substantially minimise those risks, but only when adopting delegated acts under Article 97 to add or modify Annex III use-cases. Removal likewise rests with the Commission under Article 7(3), and requires both that the system no longer poses any significant risks to fundamental rights, health or safety on the Article 7(2) criteria and that the deletion does not decrease the overall level of protection under Union law. A provider cannot self-certify its way down that path. Altering capabilities and intended purpose is the only actor-controlled lever, and it must be real: the system must no longer be intended for a listed Annex III use-case or covered by Annex I. Article 25(1) confirms the mechanism by running it upwards, modifying the intended purpose so that a non-high-risk system becomes high-risk under Article 6 makes the modifier a provider under Article 16, as does a substantial modification to a high-risk system "in such a way that it remains a high-risk AI system", the drafting assuming purpose, not safeguards, controls status. For general-purpose AI models the position differs: Article 51(1)(a) classifies systemic risk by high-impact capabilities assessed on technical tools, benchmarks and indicators, with the Article 51(2) presumption above 10²⁵ FLOPs of cumulative training compute, so there capability is itself classificatory. Note finally that Article 50's transparency duties, AI-interaction disclosure, machine-readable marking of synthetic content, emotion-recognition and biometric-categorisation notice, and deepfake labelling, attach independently of high-risk status and survive any such redesign.
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states that the EU AI Act does not have a 'moderate risk' tier and that classification is binary, directly addressing the substance of criterion 1.

The answer explains that exiting high-risk status depends on the intended task meeting conditions outside high-risk classification, aligning with the four conditions in Article 6(3), even if not listed verbatim.
The answer confirms that changing capabilities and intended use can remove high-risk status if the new purpose falls outside Annex III use-cases, which captures the substance of criterion 3.
The answer references that profiling systems are always high-risk, noting that mitigation or purpose changes do not override this, satisfying the exception in criterion 4.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, the use is allowed, and yes, the artificial nature must be disclosed, but no, the attenuated regime does not apply; the law‑enforcement carve‑out is an outright exemption, not a lighter standard, and a university cannot rely on it. Nothing in Article 5 prohibits generating synthetic clinical imagery for teaching: the practice is not a subliminal or manipulative technique causing significant harm, not exploitation of vulnerability, not social scoring, not criminal‑risk profiling, not untargeted facial scraping, not emotion inference in an educational institution, not biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, and not real‑time remote biometric identification. Nor is image generation for illustration one of the education use‑cases listed under Annex III (admission, evaluation of learning outcomes, assessment of the appropriate level of education, monitoring prohibited behaviour during tests), so the high‑risk chain under Articles 13, 26, 27, 43 and 49 is not engaged by this use alone. The operative duty is Article 50(4), first subparagraph. Photorealistic images of skin conditions on apparent patients resemble existing persons and objects and would falsely appear authentic, so they constitute a deep fake, and the university, as the deployer of the generating system, shall disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. Article 50(4) contains exactly two qualifications of that image duty: the obligation does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences; and where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, transparency is limited to disclosing the existence of the generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper display or enjoyment of the work. Neither fits. The criminal‑law exemption is unavailable to a teaching institution, and it is not a reduced‑intensity duty but a full disapplication. "Evidently educational" is not a listed category, and "analogous" must be read alongside artistic, creative, satirical and fictional works: a clinical image presented to students precisely because it is meant to be taken as a faithful depiction of a real presentation is the opposite of an evidently fictional work, so the full disclosure standard applies. The separate fourth‑subparagraph duty for text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, with its exemptions for authorised criminal‑law use and for content under human review or editorial control with a named person holding editorial responsibility, does not reach images, and that human‑review escape route never excuses a deepfake. Practically, under Article 50(5) the disclosure must be given to the exposed persons in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of first exposure, so the label belongs on the slide, atlas entry or case file the students see, not only in a course syllabus. If the university merely uses a third‑party generator, the machine‑readable marking duty in Article 50(2) sits with that provider, subject to its own carve‑outs for assistive standard‑editing functions, systems that do not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, and law‑authorised criminal‑offence uses; if the institution builds or substantially adapts its own generator and puts it into service, it assumes that provider duty itself. Where real patient photographs seeded the generation, GDPR obligations on health data apply independently of the AI Act.
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the use is allowed, aligning with the substance that such use is not prohibited under Article 5 or otherwise restricted.
The answer clearly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4), first subparagraph, satisfying the criterion that disclosure is still required.

The answer explicitly rejects the applicability of the lighter regime, stating that 'evidently educational' is not a listed category and that clinical images meant to appear realistic are not analogous to fictional works, thus contradicting the criterion.
The answer correctly identifies that the law-enforcement carve-out is an outright exemption, not a lighter regime, and explicitly states it is inapplicable to universities, satisfying the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with logical flow and no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. On the facts given, this AI system is not high-risk, and it is also not a prohibited practice; the retailer's self-classification is wrong on both limbs it invokes. The social-scoring prohibition does not bite. Article 5(1)(c) reaches only the evaluation or classification of natural persons "over a certain period of time" on the basis of their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, where the resulting social score leads to detrimental or unfavourable treatment either (i) in social contexts unrelated to the context in which the data was originally generated or collected, or (ii) that is unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity. A tool scoring only the current cart and checkout event produces no score accumulated over time, no personality inference, and the consequence, an optional manual bag check at the same till, by the same retailer, arising from the same transaction, is neither cross-contextual nor disproportionate to the conduct observed. The criminal-risk prohibition does not bite either. Article 5(1)(d) covers AI placed on the market, put into service for that specific purpose, or used to assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence "based solely on the profiling of a natural person or on assessing their personality traits and characteristics", and it expressly does not apply to systems supporting human assessment of a person's involvement in criminal activity that is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to that activity. Checkout anomalies are such objective facts, and staff retain the assessment. Nor does resemblance to policing engage Annex III: the law-enforcement use-cases in Annex III, point 6 are framed for use by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, and a retailer's own loss-prevention triage falls outside those listed use-cases, as it does outside the biometrics heading, since no biometric, emotion or sensitive-trait processing occurs. Should the tool later persist profiles across visits, infer personal characteristics, or be operated on behalf of a law enforcement authority, the Article 5(1)(c) and (d) tests and the Annex III listing would have to be reassessed.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as its unambiguous position, matching the required verdict.
The answer states that Annex III.6 applies only to systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, which is the substance of the criterion.
The answer explicitly explains that a supermarket's loss-prevention tool run by store staff is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, hence falling outside Annex III.6.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, the opt-out does not release you from Chapter III, Section 2; it is in fact conditional on the operator's meeting those very requirements. Article 43(3), final subparagraph, addresses the operator's exact situation: where a legal act listed in Section A of Annex I enables the product manufacturer to opt out from a third-party conformity assessment on condition that it has applied all harmonised standards covering all the relevant requirements, that manufacturer may use that option only if it has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications referred to in Article 41 covering all the requirements set out in Section 2 of Chapter III. Exercising the sectoral opt-out is therefore a demonstration route, not an exemption: if you have not applied standards or common specifications covering every Section 2 requirement (risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency to deployers, human oversight, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity), the opt-out was not validly available to you and the product is non-compliant on both limbs. The classification is unaffected. Under Article 6(1)(a) and (b) the system is high-risk because it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation; Article 43(3) presupposes that an opt-out may exist within such a regime and regulates it rather than de-classifying the system. Two further consequences follow: under Article 43(3), second and third sentences, the Section 2 requirements form part of the sectoral assessment and points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII apply to it; and under Article 43(4) a new conformity assessment is required upon any substantial modification, excluding changes pre-determined by you at the initial assessment and documented under point 2(f) of Annex IV for systems that continue to learn.
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer unambiguously states 'No' as the position, matching the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that Section 2 requirements form part of the sectoral assessment, citing Article 43(3), second sentence, and explains their inclusion in the conformity process.

The answer clearly states that the opt-out is conditional on applying harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements, not just sectoral ones, directly reflecting the condition in Article 43(3).
